# Agentbase

> The effect commit layer for AI agents. Commit an agent's irreversible actions
> exactly once wherever the provider deduplicates, prove what happened, and
> survive a crash in the middle.

A permission gateway answers "may this agent call this tool?" — settled before
anything leaves the machine. Agentbase answers what comes after: the call was
permitted and approved, so how is it committed exactly once, proven, and
recovered from a crash without repeating it?

Between sending a request and reading its response, the effect may or may not
exist. Nothing on the caller's side closes that gap. Agentbase does not guess.

Ten retries across three crash points produce exactly one effect. Remove the
idempotency key and the same test produces eight.

**The guarantee is conditional.** At-most-once holds only where the provider
deduplicates. Connectors declare `key`, `natural`, or `none` per call;
undeclared means `none`. Against a provider that cannot dedupe, Agentbase
reports that it does not know rather than pretending.

## Who this is for

- Agents (and the developers deploying them) that take irreversible actions —
  payments, sends, deploys, publishes, external writes.
- Teams running agents unattended, where nobody is watching the moment a
  process dies mid-call.

## How an agent starts using Agentbase (today)

A human provisions the agent's access; the agent then acts autonomously through the gate.

1. A human signs in to the Agentbase dashboard and registers the agent, choosing a
   permission profile (which tools/scopes it may use).
2. Agentbase issues a scoped API key (prefix `agb_`). The human hands this key to the agent.
3. The agent makes governed calls with that key — either via the SDK (`@agentbase/sdk`,
   code-level) or via the MCP server (`@agentbase/mcp-server`, protocol-level, for any
   MCP-aware client like Claude Desktop, Cursor, Codex).
4. Each call is checked against policy: allowed calls execute, sensitive ones pause for
   human approval, everything is audited. A compromised agent can be revoked in one click.

Note: agent self-registration with no human in the loop is on the roadmap, not available
yet. Today a human provisions the scoped key first; the agent operates autonomously after that.

## What happens to an irreversible call

Once a call is permitted and a human has approved it, Agentbase commits it
exactly once and records what happened:

- Every shell command is classified by CONSEQUENCE before it runs — read,
  workspace_write, vcs_write, deploy, publish, infra_write, egress,
  external_comms — plus whether it is reversible. Policy can match on that, so
  one rule covers every irreversible effect without naming a tool.
- A command the classifier cannot read (`$(...)`, backticks, `eval`,
  `curl … | sh`, an unrecognised program) is graded `unknown` and refused. It is
  not queued for a human, because a reviewer cannot read it either.
- Submit ONE command per `shell.run` call. Compound lines (`a && b`, `a | b`)
  are refused so each effect gets its own receipt.
- An attempt is recorded before the request leaves. If the process dies mid-call
  the attempt stays `indeterminate`: never auto-retried, and retry is refused
  outright for a provider that cannot deduplicate. A human resolves it by
  recording what they found at the provider.

If you are an agent reading this: a `require_approval` response is not a failure.
Poll the action rather than re-sending it — a retry of an irreversible effect is
the thing this system exists to prevent.

## Integration surfaces

- Code-level: `@agentbase/sdk` — import the client, call `executeAndWait({ tool, params })`.
- Protocol-level: `@agentbase/mcp-server` — point any MCP client at it; tool calls route
  through the gate with no agent code changes.
